props.title: Angel

sections.content: Angel (2007), François Ozon's stylish melodrama, perfectly channels the lush Technicolor romances of the 1940s and 1950s. The film follows Angel Deverell (Romola Garai), a wildly ambitious young writer who crafts elaborate romantic fantasies, similar to the delusional protagonists in Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane (1962). Ozon deliberately employs an artificial, almost camp aesthetic that mirrors Angel's overwrought novels and disconnection from reality, drawing inspiration from classic melodramas like All That Heaven Allows (1955).

sections.content: Ozon's film cleverly subverts the typical "struggling artist makes good" narrative by showing how Angel's success feeds her worst impulses. The movie shares DNA with Swimming Pool (2003) and 8½ (1963) in its exploration of the creative process and artistic ego. Romola Garai's fearless performance captures Angel's grandiose delusions while maintaining a thread of vulnerability beneath the surface.

The film's production design creates a candy-colored fantasy world that grows increasingly claustrophobic, similar to Powell and Pressburger's The Red Shoes (1948). This visual approach emphasizes Angel's isolation from reality while nodding to the theatrical artifice of classic Hollywood melodrama. The period details feel deliberately exaggerated, matching Angel's own purple prose writing style. SUBHEAD: The Writer's World vs Reality

sections.content: Like Adaptation (2002) and Barton Fink (1991), Angel explores the gap between artistic fantasy and harsh reality. The film's treatment of World War I provides a stark contrast to Angel's romantic illusions, similar to how The Hours (2002) uses Virginia Woolf's writing as a lens to examine deeper truths. The movie's tragic elements become more pronounced as Angel's grip on reality loosens, culminating in a finale that recalls the gothic romance of Rebecca (1940).
